Closing down on the Guptas

By: Este de Klerk | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
They're known for their power, money and influence, but who exactly are the Guptas?

Further information:
In several media interviews, the middle of the three Gupta brothers, Atul, was quoted to say that their late father, Shiv Kumar Gupta sent him to South Africa in 1993, believing that Africa was about to become the “America of the world” – the world’s land of opportunity.

Former Cosatu Secretary general, Zwelinzima Vavi has called the Guptas South Africa’s shadow government. And as the country was facing the worst economic crisis in December since 2009, the Guptas became a scapegoat, alongside President Jacob Zuma.

EFF leader, Julius Malema coined the phrase “Zupta” as he sought to underscore how President Zuma and the Guptas were in cahoots and demanded they leave the country for allegedly benefiting unduly off government contracts because of their chumminess to the President.

Political analysts are warning that the democracy of our country is being undermind – especially after it came to light that the Guptas made offers of becoming Cabinet Ministers to former ANC-MP and former chairperson of the portfolio committee on Public Works, Vytjie Mentoor, and deputy-finance Minister, Mcebisi Jonas – allegations still denied by the Guptas. This lead to an internal ANC investigation led by Secretary General Gwede Mantashe, investigating the influence of the Guptas on government.

And on Thursday, Malema’s wish may well have come true – Aptul and Ajah have reportedly left the country via the Lanseria airport in Johannesburg late on Thursday night on their private jet, taking off with a flight plan scheduled to land 37km from Dubai. On Friday, all the Guptas, together with Zuma’s son, Duduzane, resigned as shareholders of the Gupta’s Oakbay Investments and Resources and on Monday it was reported that they have flown to Uttar Prakesh in India, where they are originally from.

But who are the Guptas – the three brothers, Ajay (55), Atul (47) and Rajesh (43) and how did they land up in South Africa? And how was it possible for them to have so much political power, especially when it come to our President?

- they and their sister, Achla, were raised in the city Saharanpur in North India by their father, Shiv and mother, Angoori
- they weren’t raised in poverty and their father was one of the only residents in the city of 700 000 people, who owned a car
- Shiv imported spices from Madagascar and Zanzibar and sold it in India
- Shiv sent Atul to South Africa in 1993
- In 1994, the same year in which his father died, Atul opened a shoe-shop called the Liberty Da Trend-boetiek in the Killarney shopping Mall. But it failed
- Next, also in 1994, he started a company called “Correct Marketing”, importing computers
- By 1997, Correct Marketing had an overturn of R9 million per year and the name was changed to “Sahara Computers”
- According to Mail & Guardian part of their fortune happened when they got a contract to supply government departments with computers, as well ass a tender to supply 300 000 laptops to teachers
- Ajay, the eldest brother, is the head of the family and takes all the financial decisions
- They all live on the R52 million Saxonwold Sahara estate in Johannesburg, but also have houses in Durban and Constantia, Cape Town – the house that once belonged to Mark Thatcher, son of Margaret Thatcher
- They have met Zuma about ten years ago at a Sahara event
- Zuma’s son, Duduzane started to work at Sahara at the age of 22 and quickly became Rajesh’s associate in Mabengela Investments
- Jacob Zuma’s wife, Bongi Ngema-Zuma worked at the Gupta-controlled JIC Mining Services in public relations
- Zuma’s daughter, Duduzile served on the Board of Sahara Computers in 2007 and 2009

The Guptas at a glance
• Ajay, Atul and Rajesh Gupta moved to South African from India in 1993
• Atul is said to have set up their first business Sahara Computers, which now has an annual turnover of 200m rand ($22m; £14.3m)
• Business interests also include air travel, energy, technology and media
• No clear indication of their net worth – they are not featured on any list of the continent’s richest

The Gupta family’s business empire in SA, which centres on information technology, mining and media, is heavily dependent on political connections. Because much of it is unlisted, it would be difficult to price if they wished to exit, particularly under current weak market conditions for mining and media.

The oldest business is Sahara Holdings, which was begun by brothers Atul, Anil and Rajesh about 20 years ago. It assembles and markets PCs and sells consumables. Sahara’s empowerment partners include Afripalm, headed by Lazarus Zim, and Mvelaphanda Resources, which was founded by Tokyo Sexwale.

In mining, the Gupta family holds interests through Oakbay Investments in contract miner JIC, Shiva Uranium (in which Duduzane Zuma was a director until Friday) and Tegeta Exploration and Resources.
Shiva and Tegeta are part of JSE-listed Oakbay Resources and Energy. Tegeta owns the Brakfontein coal mine which supplies state-owned Eskom and recently agreed to buy the Optimum Coal mine, an Eskom supplier, from Glencore. Shiva Uranium was bought with a R250m loan from the state-owned Industrial Development Corporation.

Although it is speculated that Shiva Uranium is positioning itself to supply SA’s planned nuclear power stations, it is only mining gold, not uranium at Dominion mine, because uranium prices are too low.

The business rescue practitioners behind the rescue plan for Optimum Coal Mine are confident Tegeta can continue with plans to buy Optimum. Sources close to the deal indicated the necessary funding had been secured. The deal will be concluded only once the purchase price has been paid.
Although the Guptas have resigned their directorships of the Oakbay companies the family remains the controlling shareholder with an estimated 68%.

Press Release:


Who are the Guptas?
From multi-billion rand business interests, to a wedding party landing at a national key point and a President seemingly under their influence. Who are the Guptas really? Carte Blanche takes an in-depth look into the lives of SA’s most controversial family.


Script:


WHO ARE THE GUPTAS?

PRODUCER: ESTÉ DE KLERK

SOLLY MAPAILA: They seen as untouchables.

FERIAL HAFFAJEE: Wherever the state had a big hand you would see they would go and open up a new entry point there.

PRINCE MASHELE: These people still have big plans to further capture the state.

The Gupta family has been called South Africa’s “shadow government” because of their apparent ties with President Jacob Zuma, his son and other high-level politicians. Accused of wielding enormous political influence in South Africa, critics say they are “capturing the state” to advance their own interests.

A former employee who wanted his identity hidden, says that was the way they did business.

INSIDER: They had private dinners and they did have guests coming to functions at home. They would invite a large number of prominent guests – Ministers and Cabinet Ministers with various portfolios would attend at times. There was a big emphasis on being able to be included in this country that they’d invested in. They really sincerely believed in what they were doing. I don’t think they believed there was anything wrong with any of it.

DEVI LINK: They are known for their power, influence and money. But who exactly are the Guptas? A family who have, in just 23 years, rose up from selling shoes from the boot of their car to having to significant influence on the most powerful man in our country.

Since the beginning of the year, it seemed as if the web was slowly, but surely closing in on the Guptas.
Opposition parties, organised labour and high-ranking politicians have recently made bold moves.

But a defiant move came from an unexpected quarter – shutting off access to the accounts of their businesses, including their first venture Sahara Holdings.

DEVI LINK: Then, within three months, four of South Africa’s largest banks wrote to the Guptas informing them they will no longer do business with the family or their associated companies.

City Press editor, Ferial Haffajee says depending on who you speak to, the Guptas are either a glowing success story OR the beneficiaries of their political connections.

FERIAL HAFFAJEE: So imagine how this must have gone down … all your bankers are sending you letters… they sending letters to all your varied companies. If you look here The Guptas owned shares in about 40 companies and not just the two that they resigned directorships of - and that there is Oakbay the biggest part of their corporate empire.

DEVI LINK: On Thursday evening, the 7th of April, Atul and Ajay left on their private plane from Lanseria airport to Dubai.

On Wednesday, a source close to the Guptas confirmed that the entire family, including their mother, wives and children had indeed left from Lanseria airport on Thursday night.
The youngest brother, Rajesh has been living in Dubai for some months.

Our insider says it would have been Ajay who made the decision to leave.

INSIDER: He took over as some kind of patriarch when their father died. He was the facilitator and kind of dealmaker and he would be very disarming in his business dealings, but if he was angered in any way he would have a really volatile temper exploding often and becoming menacing

A day after they left, Atul and Ajay resigned all their directorships in their Oakbay Group. And so did their business associate, President Zuma’s son, Duduzane, who was a director of twelve companies in the Gupta empire.

It’s been reported that the Gupta’s shareholdings are now in the safekeeping of local executives.

DEVI LINK: Our repeated telephone calls, sms’s and emails to Nazeem Howa, CEO of Oakbay resources, were ignored.

Political analyst, Prince Mashele says the Guptas’ resignations were merely a tactical move – they still own the majority of shares in their companies.

PRINCE MASHELE: They are not totally out of South Africa. All they are doing is a tactic to make us rest on our laurels and we must not do that.

DEVI LINK: The Guptas have amassed a fortune with their business interests ranging from engineering and mining to IT, a 24-hour television station and a daily newspaper.

But they come from humble beginnings. From a decrepit building in Saharapur in India - where they were unknown - to a mansion in Saxonwold, Johannesburg.
Sunday Times senior journalist, Prega Govender.

PREGA: Their father opened a business in Delhi SKG Marketing where he imported spices from Zanzibar and Madagascar.

DEVI LINK 5: Shiv Kumar Gupta send his son, Atul to South Africa in 1993, because he believed Africa would be the “America of the world”.

Atul first imported shoes from India, but this venture failed. And then in 1994, his father transferred R1,2 million into his bank account in South Africa.

PREGA GOVENDER: Atul used the money to start up CORRECT MARKETING a business specializing in sale of computers. In 1997 CM became Sahara computers. Turnover in 94 was R1.4 million. It skyrocketed to 97 million in 1997.

In the same year, Rajesh was also sent to South Africa and in 2000, the rest of the family followed. It was Rajesh who first became friends with President Zuma’s son, Duduzane.

The Guptas were relatively unknown in political circles until the early 2000s when former Minister of Information and Communications in the Presidency, E ssop Pahad met Rajesh Gupta.

FERIAL: The Gupta family were the key supporters and sponsors of the Thinker magazines which Minister Pahad published after he left govt service. That’s when they got into Big Politics.

INSIDER: At the time of Polokwane, Sahara Computers provided all the communications and all of the computers for ANC delegates and the convention. The marketing manager at the time, just mentioned that Kgalema Mothlanthe was very president like and was likely to be the next President. Low and behold, a few weeks later he was President. And that’s when I got my first inkling of how well connected it all seemed to be.

The family’s introduction to the ANC top structure, including President Zuma himself, followed.

INSIDER: They suddenly switched when Jacob Zuma started to ascend in terms of the likelihood of him becoming president. The focus seemed to shift.

PREGA: When asked about it, Atul told me at the time: “Please tell us about any unfair benefit which the Gupta family had by Zuma.” He categorically stated there was no such relationship.

After he was elected, President Zuma frequently visited the Gupta’s homes in Saxonwold.

INSIDER: He came fairly often. I seem to rememeber It was usually on a Thursday and he often stayed for a meal.

Our insider tells us that the Guptas, on occasion, made special arrangements for the President and other high-profile officals.


INSIDER: No-one questioned these moves, as this was the usual kind of method that was used.

PRINCE MASHELE: Remember the Philosopher Plato once said philosopher kings must not have families, because that diverts their attention from state affairs. Here is a philosopher king who has a large army of children. The Guptas understood that this guy can’t afford to support his children.

In the March, 18th-publication of the Gupta-owned newspaper, the New Age, the family stated that it was “absurd to suggest that” they benefitted from government business when less than 1% of the Group’s business was with the government”.

Shortly before, Deputy Finance Minister Mcebisi Jonas made his shock anouncement.

MCEBISI JONAS: Members of the Gupta-family offered me the position of Minister of Finance to replace then Minister Nene. I rejected this out of hand.

DEVI LINK: Mcebisi Jonas’s revelation was the first public confirmation from a high-ranking Minister that there was indeed a very strong link between President Jacob Zuma and the Gupta family.

The Guptas denied making the offer, just as they denied offering Vytjie Mentor the post of Public Enterprises Minister in 2010.

INSIDER: They talk around issue and lead the person to believe that is what will happen if certain conditions are fulfilled, but they never say it directly.

The ANC then launched a formal investigation into the Gupas’ activities.
But the SACP’s Solly Mapaila says government’s investigation was long-overdue. The SACP has raised the issue with the ANC every year for the last four years and also met with President Zuma on the subject.

SOLLY: In this case, because of the level of contamination and the poisonous nature of the relationship, the impact it is having on the unit of the ANC and the alliance. He has to chose between the Guptas and the SA revolution which is led by the ANC which he leads.

The SACP has asked for a judicial commission of inquiry to be established.

FERIAL HAFFAJEE: Faced with the investigation with media, with media reporting, with people standing outside their house – it felt to me that this was a family who just said enough.




INSIDER: Their first reaction would have been anger at suggestions that they have done anything improper. The way they conducted themselves has been the way they have been doing things ever since they started their businesses and I don’t believe they believe that there’s anything untoward about it. They would have believed that there was some grouping with an ulterior motive that was trying to sabotage them.

The termination of their banking services has placed the Gupta family in a precarious position. And even as Nazeem Howa was scrambling to restore banking relationships this week, it has already been reported that one bank declined to meet with him.

INSIDER: They have mercurial personalities and they don't take kindly if they are crossed. They base a lot of their dealings on a level of trust with whomever they’re dealing with. There is a good chance that once you’re out, you’re out and off that list.

The Gupta’s abrupt exit from the country, has however left a trail of questions.

FERIAL HAFFAJEE: I don't’ think it is the end of the Guptas as is been the narrative. I think what they will become now is part of the global elite – the global rich who move around the world to their very different homes and their businesses interests.

PRINCE: The Guptas still have the power to damage and destroy the country.


PROMO’S

They are known for their power, influence and money. But who exactly are the Guptas?
There was a big emphasis on being able to be included in this country that they’d invested in. They really sincerely believed in what they were doing. I don’t think they believed there was anything wrong with any of it.

INSIDER

PROMO 2: 15”
INSIDER: They talk around issue and lead the person to believe that is what will happen if certain conditions are fulfilled, but they never say it directly.

Power, influence and money - how did the Gupta’s rise up so quickly?

PROMO 3: 10”

INSIDER: No-one questioned these moves, because this was the usual kind of method that was used.

PRINCE: The Guptas still have the power to damage and destroy the country.

Since the beginning of the year, it seemed as if the web was slowly, but surely closing in on the Guptas. Opposition parties, organised labour and high-ranking politicians have recently made bold moves. But a defiant move came from an unexpected quarter – shutting off access to the accounts of their businesses, including their first venture Sahara Holdings. DEVI LINK: Then, within three months, four of South Africa’s largest banks wrote to the Guptas informing them they will no longer do business with the family or their associated companies. City Press editor, Ferial Haffajee says depending on who you speak to, the Guptas are either a glowing success story OR the beneficiaries of their political connections. FERIAL HAFFAJEE: So imagine how this must have gone down … all your bankers are sending you letters… they sending letters to all your varied companies. If you look here The Guptas owned shares in about 40 companies and not just the two that they resigned directorships of - and that there is Oakbay the biggest part of their corporate empire. DEVI LINK: On Thursday evening, the 7th of April, Atul and Ajay left on their private plane from Lanseria airport to Dubai. On Wednesday, a source close to the Guptas confirmed that the entire family, including their mother, wives and children had indeed left from Lanseria airport on Thursday night. The youngest brother, Rajesh has been living in Dubai for some months. Our insider says it would have been Ajay who made the decision to leave. INSIDER: He took over as some kind of patriarch when their father died. He was the facilitator and kind of dealmaker and he would be very disarming in his business dealings, but if he was angered in any way he would have a really volatile temper exploding often and becoming menacing A day after they left, Atul and Ajay resigned all their directorships in their Oakbay Group. And so did their business associate, President Zuma’s son, Duduzane, who was a director of twelve companies in the Gupta empire. It’s been reported that the Gupta’s shareholdings are now in the safekeeping of local executives. DEVI LINK: Our repeated telephone calls, sms’s and emails to Nazeem Howa, CEO of Oakbay resources, were ignored. Political analyst, Prince Mashele says the Guptas’ resignations were merely a tactical move – they still own the majority of shares in their companies. PRINCE MASHELE: They are not totally out of South Africa. All they are doing is a tactic to make us rest on our laurels and we must not do that. DEVI LINK: The Guptas have amassed a fortune with their business interests ranging from engineering and mining to IT, a 24-hour television station and a daily newspaper. But they come from humble beginnings. From a decrepit building in Saharapur in India - where they were unknown - to a mansion in Saxonwold, Johannesburg. Sunday Times senior journalist, Prega Govender. PREGA: Their father opened a business in Delhi SKG Marketing where he imported spices from Zanzibar and Madagascar. DEVI LINK 5: Shiv Kumar Gupta send his son, Atul to South Africa in 1993, because he believed Africa would be the “America of the world”. Atul first imported shoes from India, but this venture failed. And then in 1994, his father transferred R1,2 million into his bank account in South Africa. PREGA GOVENDER: Atul used the money to start up CORRECT MARKETING a business specializing in sale of computers. In 1997 CM became Sahara computers. Turnover in 94 was R1.4 million. It skyrocketed to 97 million in 1997. In the same year, Rajesh was also sent to South Africa and in 2000, the rest of the family followed. It was Rajesh who first became friends with President Zuma’s son, Duduzane. The Guptas were relatively unknown in political circles until the early 2000s when former Minister of Information and Communications in the Presidency, E ssop Pahad met Rajesh Gupta. FERIAL: The Gupta family were the key supporters and sponsors of the Thinker magazines which Minister Pahad published after he left govt service. That’s when they got into Big Politics. INSIDER: At the time of Polokwane, Sahara Computers provided all the communications and all of the computers for ANC delegates and the convention. The marketing manager at the time, just mentioned that Kgalema Mothlanthe was very president like and was likely to be the next President. Low and behold, a few weeks later he was President. And that’s when I got my first inkling of how well connected it all seemed to be. The family’s introduction to the ANC top structure, including President Zuma himself, followed. INSIDER: They suddenly switched when Jacob Zuma started to ascend in terms of the likelihood of him becoming president. The focus seemed to shift. PREGA: When asked about it, Atul told me at the time: “Please tell us about any unfair benefit which the Gupta family had by Zuma.” He categorically stated there was no such relationship. After he was elected, President Zuma frequently visited the Gupta’s homes in Saxonwold. INSIDER: He came fairly often. I seem to rememeber It was usually on a Thursday and he often stayed for a meal. Our insider tells us that the Guptas, on occasion, made special arrangements for the President and other high-profile officals. INSIDER: No-one questioned these moves, as this was the usual kind of method that was used. PRINCE MASHELE: Remember the Philosopher Plato once said philosopher kings must not have families, because that diverts their attention from state affairs. Here is a philosopher king who has a large army of children. The Guptas understood that this guy can’t afford to support his children. In the March, 18th-publication of the Gupta-owned newspaper, the New Age, the family stated that it was “absurd to suggest that” they benefitted from government business when less than 1% of the Group’s business was with the government”. Shortly before, Deputy Finance Minister Mcebisi Jonas made his shock anouncement. MCEBISI JONAS: Members of the Gupta-family offered me the position of Minister of Finance to replace then Minister Nene. I rejected this out of hand. DEVI LINK: Mcebisi Jonas’s revelation was the first public confirmation from a high-ranking Minister that there was indeed a very strong link between President Jacob Zuma and the Gupta family. The Guptas denied making the offer, just as they denied offering Vytjie Mentor the post of Public Enterprises Minister in 2010. INSIDER: They talk around issue and lead the person to believe that is what will happen if certain conditions are fulfilled, but they never say it directly. The ANC then launched a formal investigation into the Gupas’ activities. But the SACP’s Solly Mapaila says government’s investigation was long-overdue. The SACP has raised the issue with the ANC every year for the last four years and also met with President Zuma on the subject. SOLLY: In this case, because of the level of contamination and the poisonous nature of the relationship, the impact it is having on the unit of the ANC and the alliance. He has to chose between the Guptas and the SA revolution which is led by the ANC which he leads. The SACP has asked for a judicial commission of inquiry to be established. FERIAL HAFFAJEE: Faced with the investigation with media, with media reporting, with people standing outside their house – it felt to me that this was a family who just said enough. INSIDER: Their first reaction would have been anger at suggestions that they have done anything improper. The way they conducted themselves has been the way they have been doing things ever since they started their businesses and I don’t believe they believe that there’s anything untoward about it. They would have believed that there was some grouping with an ulterior motive that was trying to sabotage them. The termination of their banking services has placed the Gupta family in a precarious position. And even as Nazeem Howa was scrambling to restore banking relationships this week, it has already been reported that one bank declined to meet with him. INSIDER: They have mercurial personalities and they don't take kindly if they are crossed. They base a lot of their dealings on a level of trust with whomever they’re dealing with. There is a good chance that once you’re out, you’re out and off that list. The Gupta’s abrupt exit from the country, has however left a trail of questions. FERIAL HAFFAJEE: I don't’ think it is the end of the Guptas as is been the narrative. I think what they will become now is part of the global elite – the global rich who move around the world to their very different homes and their businesses interests. PRINCE: The Guptas still have the power to damage and destroy the country. PROMO’S They are known for their power, influence and money. But who exactly are the Guptas? There was a big emphasis on being able to be included in this country that they’d invested in. They really sincerely believed in what they were doing. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): They're known for their power, money and influence, but who exactly are the Guptas?
metadata.Further information: In several media interviews, the middle of the three Gupta brothers, Atul, was quoted to say that their late father, Shiv Kumar Gupta sent him to South Africa in 1993, believing that Africa was about to become the “America of the world” – the world’s land of opportunity. Former Cosatu Secretary general, Zwelinzima Vavi has called the Guptas South Africa’s shadow government. And as the country was facing the worst economic crisis in December since 2009, the Guptas became a scapegoat, alongside President Jacob Zuma. EFF leader, Julius Malema coined the phrase “Zupta” as he sought to underscore how President Zuma and the Guptas were in cahoots and demanded they leave the country for allegedly benefiting unduly off government contracts because of their chumminess to the President. Political analysts are warning that the democracy of our country is being undermind – especially after it came to light that the Guptas made offers of becoming Cabinet Ministers to former ANC-MP and former chairperson of the portfolio committee on Public Works, Vytjie Mentoor, and deputy-finance Minister, Mcebisi Jonas – allegations still denied by the Guptas. This lead to an internal ANC investigation led by Secretary General Gwede Mantashe, investigating the influence of the Guptas on government. And on Thursday, Malema’s wish may well have come true – Aptul and Ajah have reportedly left the country via the Lanseria airport in Johannesburg late on Thursday night on their private jet, taking off with a flight plan scheduled to land 37km from Dubai. On Friday, all the Guptas, together with Zuma’s son, Duduzane, resigned as shareholders of the Gupta’s Oakbay Investments and Resources and on Monday it was reported that they have flown to Uttar Prakesh in India, where they are originally from. But who are the Guptas – the three brothers, Ajay (55), Atul (47) and Rajesh (43) and how did they land up in South Africa? And how was it possible for them to have so much political power, especially when it come to our President? - they and their sister, Achla, were raised in the city Saharanpur in North India by their father, Shiv and mother, Angoori - they weren’t raised in poverty and their father was one of the only residents in the city of 700 000 people, who owned a car - Shiv imported spices from Madagascar and Zanzibar and sold it in India - Shiv sent Atul to South Africa in 1993 - In 1994, the same year in which his father died, Atul opened a shoe-shop called the Liberty Da Trend-boetiek in the Killarney shopping Mall. But it failed - Next, also in 1994, he started a company called “Correct Marketing”, importing computers - By 1997, Correct Marketing had an overturn of R9 million per year and the name was changed to “Sahara Computers” - According to Mail & Guardian part of their fortune happened when they got a contract to supply government departments with computers, as well ass a tender to supply 300 000 laptops to teachers - Ajay, the eldest brother, is the head of the family and takes all the financial decisions - They all live on the R52 million Saxonwold Sahara estate in Johannesburg, but also have houses in Durban and Constantia, Cape Town – the house that once belonged to Mark Thatcher, son of Margaret Thatcher - They have met Zuma about ten years ago at a Sahara event - Zuma’s son, Duduzane started to work at Sahara at the age of 22 and quickly became Rajesh’s associate in Mabengela Investments - Jacob Zuma’s wife, Bongi Ngema-Zuma worked at the Gupta-controlled JIC Mining Services in public relations - Zuma’s daughter, Duduzile served on the Board of Sahara Computers in 2007 and 2009 The Guptas at a glance • Ajay, Atul and Rajesh Gupta moved to South African from India in 1993 • Atul is said to have set up their first business Sahara Computers, which now has an annual turnover of 200m rand ($22m; £14.3m) • Business interests also include air travel, energy, technology and media • No clear indication of their net worth – they are not featured on any list of the continent’s richest The Gupta family’s business empire in SA, which centres on information technology, mining and media, is heavily dependent on political connections. Because much of it is unlisted, it would be difficult to price if they wished to exit, particularly under current weak market conditions for mining and media. The oldest business is Sahara Holdings, which was begun by brothers Atul, Anil and Rajesh about 20 years ago. It assembles and markets PCs and sells consumables. Sahara’s empowerment partners include Afripalm, headed by Lazarus Zim, and Mvelaphanda Resources, which was founded by Tokyo Sexwale. In mining, the Gupta family holds interests through Oakbay Investments in contract miner JIC, Shiva Uranium (in which Duduzane Zuma was a director until Friday) and Tegeta Exploration and Resources. Shiva and Tegeta are part of JSE-listed Oakbay Resources and Energy. Tegeta owns the Brakfontein coal mine which supplies state-owned Eskom and recently agreed to buy the Optimum Coal mine, an Eskom supplier, from Glencore. Shiva Uranium was bought with a R250m loan from the state-owned Industrial Development Corporation. Although it is speculated that Shiva Uranium is positioning itself to supply SA’s planned nuclear power stations, it is only mining gold, not uranium at Dominion mine, because uranium prices are too low. The business rescue practitioners behind the rescue plan for Optimum Coal Mine are confident Tegeta can continue with plans to buy Optimum. Sources close to the deal indicated the necessary funding had been secured. The deal will be concluded only once the purchase price has been paid. Although the Guptas have resigned their directorships of the Oakbay companies the family remains the controlling shareholder with an estimated 68%.
